lesson.title: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law: The Circuit's Return to Zero
lesson.summary: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law says the voltage rises and drops around any closed loop must sum to zero, a direct consequence of energy conservation that underlies every loop-based circuit technique.
lesson.body:
Imagine walking a loop through a circuit and keeping a running tally of every voltage rise and drop you pass. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law, or KVL, says that when you get back to your starting point, that tally must equal exactly zero. This is not a coincidence or a convenient approximation, it is a direct consequence of energy conservation. Voltage is potential energy per unit charge, so if you carry a charge all the way around a closed loop and return to the exact point you started, the net change in its potential energy has to be zero, because potential energy is a property of position, not of the path taken to get there.

To apply KVL formally, pick a direction to trace around a loop, clockwise or counterclockwise, either works, and assign a sign to each element you cross: if you move from the minus terminal to the plus terminal of a source, that is a voltage rise; if you move through a resistor in the direction of assumed current flow, that is a voltage drop. Add up all the rises and drops with consistent signs, set the sum to zero, and solve. The law holds for any loop in any circuit, linear or nonlinear, and it does not care what the elements actually are, only that the loop closes.

Consider a single loop with a 12 volt source and three resistors in series: R1 equals 2 ohms, R2 equals 3 ohms, and R3 equals 7 ohms. Because it is a series circuit, the same current I flows through every element, so the total resistance is 2 plus 3 plus 7, which is 12 ohms. By Ohm's law, I equals 12 volts divided by 12 ohms, or 1 amp. The voltage drop across each resistor is then V1 equals 1 times 2, or 2 volts, V2 equals 1 times 3, or 3 volts, and V3 equals 1 times 7, or 7 volts. Tracing the loop starting at the source: a rise of 12 volts through the source, then drops of 2, 3, and 7 volts through the resistors. Written as a KVL equation, negative 12 plus 2 plus 3 plus 7 equals zero, and indeed 2 plus 3 plus 7 is exactly 12, so the equation balances.

This example is really the derivation of the series voltage divider in disguise: KVL is the reason the source voltage always equals the sum of the individual drops in a series circuit, no more and no less. That relationship only feels obvious after you have seen why it must be true. The same bookkeeping generalizes far beyond simple series loops. When circuits have multiple loops sharing branches, KVL applied to each independent loop, together with Kirchhoff's Current Law at the nodes, gives you exactly enough equations to solve for every unknown current and voltage in the circuit, which is the entire foundation of the mesh current method covered later in this chapter.

One subtlety worth internalizing now: KVL does not require you to already know the correct direction of current or the correct sign of a voltage. You can guess a direction, write the equation, and solve. If a current or voltage comes out negative, that simply means the real direction is opposite to your guess. The law itself never fails, only your bookkeeping can, so getting comfortable with consistent sign conventions here pays off in every analysis technique that follows.
